statement: Let $R>0$ and let $f$ be [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disk $|z|\le R$, with values in a complex normed space, with finite order at every point. With $C_w(z)=\frac{R^2-\bar w z}{R(z-w)}$ there is a function $g$, meromorphic in normal form and zero-free on $|z|<R$, such that $f=\big(\prod_{|w|<R}C_w^{-\operatorname{ord}_w f}\big)\,g$ off a discrete set.

hypotheses.text: The radius $R$ is positive.
The function $f$ is [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disk $|z|\le R$.
The function $f$ is [locally nonzero](c:locally-nonzero-function) at every point of the closed disk, so its order is never $\infty$.

conclusion: There is a function $g$, meromorphic in normal form on the closed disk and zero-free on the open disk, with $f=\big(\prod_{|w|<R}C_w^{-\operatorname{ord}_w f}\big)\,g$ outside a discrete subset of the closed disk.

formal.difference: mathlib allows any real $R$ and treats $R\le 0$ as a trivial case with an empty open disk. Otherwise the statements agree.

proofs.name: Cancel by canonical factors
proofs.slogan: Multiply f by canonical factors that cancel its zeros and poles, then pass to the normal form.
proofs.scope: The case $R>0$. For $R\le 0$ the open disk is empty: take $g$ constant equal to $f(0)$ and the product empty.

roles.why: A positive radius makes the open disk nonempty and defines every canonical factor.
Meromorphy of $f$ gives a meromorphic product and only finitely many zeros and poles.
Finite order everywhere lets orders add, so the product has order $0$ at each point of the open disk.

steps.slogan: Show that each canonical factor has one simple pole and no zero.
steps.detail: For $|w|<R$ and $|z|\le R$ we have $|R^2-\bar w z|\ge R^2-|w|R>0$, so $C_w$ has no zero on the closed disk. Its only [pole](c:pole-of-a-function) is $z=w$ and it is simple, because the numerator is nonzero there. So $\operatorname{ord}_w C_w=-1$ and $\operatorname{ord}_z C_w=0$ for $z\ne w$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ has only finitely many zeros and poles in the open disk.
steps.detail: Near a point $p$ the function is $(z-p)^k h(z)$ with $h$ nonzero at $p$, because its order is finite. So the points with nonzero order have no accumulation point in the closed disk. A compact disk holds only finitely many of them, so $n(w)=\operatorname{ord}_w f$ is nonzero for finitely many $w$.

steps.slogan: Multiply $f$ by the finite product of the canonical factors raised to $n(w)$.
steps.detail: Put $\varphi=\big(\prod_w C_w^{n(w)}\big)f$, a finite product. At a point $w$ with $n(w)\ne 0$, the factor $C_w^{n(w)}$ has order $-n(w)$ and $f$ has order $n(w)$, so $\varphi$ has order $0$. At every other point of the open disk all factors have order $0$, so the order of $\varphi$ is that of $f$, which is $0$.

steps.slogan: Replace $\varphi$ by its meromorphic normal form $g$.
steps.detail: Changing $\varphi$ on a discrete set gives a function $g$ in normal form with the same orders at every point. At a point of the open disk the order is $0$, so $g$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) there and $g(z)\ne 0$. The set where $g\ne\varphi$ is discrete.

steps.slogan: Multiply back by the inverse product to recover $f$ off a discrete set.
steps.detail: Away from the finitely many $w$ with $n(w)\ne 0$, $C_w^{-n(w)}C_w^{n(w)}=1$ pointwise. Hence $f=\big(\prod_w C_w^{-n(w)}\big)\varphi$ there, and $\varphi=g$ off a discrete set. The excluded points form a discrete set, which gives the stated identity.

concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The product of meromorphic functions is meromorphic and has a well-defined order.
concepts.c:locally-nonzero-function: A locally nonzero function has finite order, so orders add under multiplication.
concepts.c:pole-of-a-function: Each canonical factor contributes exactly one simple pole, which cancels one zero of $f$.
concepts.c:analytic-function: Order $0$ in normal form means $g$ is analytic and nonzero at the point.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle) with [circumcenter](c:circumcenter) $D$, circumradius $R$ and [inradius](c:inradius) $r$. The signed distances from $D$ to the three sides sum to $R+r$. A distance is negative exactly when the open segment from $D$ to the foot lies outside the triangle.

hypotheses.text: The points $A,B,C$ form a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle) with angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

conclusion: The signed distances $d_a,d_b,d_c$ from $D$ to $BC,CA,AB$ satisfy $d_a+d_b+d_c=R+r$.

proofs.name: Trigonometric identity
proofs.slogan: Write each signed distance as $R\cos$ of an angle, then compare the cosine sum with the inradius.
proofs.scope: All triangles, acute, right or obtuse. A right angle gives distance $0$, matching $\cos 90^\circ=0$.

roles.why: The triangle fixes the angles with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^\circ$, the circumcircle of radius $R$ and the incircle of radius $r$.

steps.slogan: Show that the signed distance from $D$ to $BC$ equals $R\cos\alpha$.
steps.detail: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, the foot of the perpendicular from $D$. If $\alpha<90^\circ$, the [inscribed angle](c:inscribed-angle) theorem gives $\angle BDC=2\alpha$ with $D$ on the side of $A$, so $DM=R\cos\alpha$. If $\alpha>90^\circ$, then $D$ lies across $BC$, $DM=-R\cos\alpha$ and the signed distance $-DM$ is $R\cos\alpha$; if $\alpha=90^\circ$, then $D=M$ and both values are $0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the three cosines sum to $1+4\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}$.
steps.detail: Since $\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}=90^\circ-\frac{\gamma}{2}$, we get $\cos\alpha+\cos\beta=2\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$, and $\cos\gamma=1-2\sin^2\frac{\gamma}{2}$ with $\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}=\cos\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$. The sum is $1+2\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\big(\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}-\cos\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\big)$, and the bracket equals $2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the inradius equals $4R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}$.
steps.detail: The incircle touches $BC$ at $X$ with $BX=r\cot\frac{\beta}{2}$ and $XC=r\cot\frac{\gamma}{2}$, so $a=r\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}\big/\big(\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\big)$. The law of sines gives $a=2R\sin\alpha=4R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}$. Equate the two values of $a$.

steps.slogan: Add the three distances and replace the cosine sum by the inradius formula.
steps.detail: By the first step, $d_a+d_b+d_c=R(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma)$. By the second step this is $R+4R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}$. By the third step the last term is $r$, so the sum is $R+r$.

concepts.c:triangle: Its angles sum to $180^\circ$, which links the half-angles in the identities.
concepts.c:circumcenter: The circumcenter is the point whose distances to the sides are summed.
concepts.c:inradius: The inradius is the second term of the sum and has a half-angle formula.
concepts.c:inscribed-angle: It turns the angle at $A$ into the central angle $\angle BDC$.

source.note: Standard trigonometric proof through the half-angle formula for the inradius.

statement: Let $G$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group). Then $G$ is [simple](c:simple-group) if and only if its order is a [prime number](c:prime-number). Such a group is [cyclic](c:cyclic-group).

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is [abelian](c:abelian-group).

conclusion: $G$ is [simple](c:simple-group) exactly when $|G|$ is prime, and then $G$ is [cyclic](c:cyclic-group).

proofs.name: Cyclic generator and Lagrange
proofs.slogan: A simple abelian group is cyclic, a generator of composite or infinite order gives a proper subgroup, and Lagrange gives the converse.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The trivial group is not simple and has no prime order. An infinite group has no prime order and is shown not simple.

roles.why: Commutativity makes every subgroup [normal](c:normal-subgroup), so simplicity says that the only subgroups are $1$ and $G$.

steps.slogan: Show that every subgroup of $G$ is normal.
steps.detail: For $x\in G$ and $h$ in a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ we have $xhx^{-1}=h$ because $G$ is abelian. So $H$ is [normal](c:normal-subgroup). Hence $G$ is simple exactly when $G\ne 1$ and its only subgroups are $1$ and $G$.

steps.slogan: Show that a simple abelian group is generated by any element other than $1$.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be simple and $g\ne 1$. The subgroup $\langle g\rangle$ is normal and nontrivial, so $\langle g\rangle=G$. Hence $G$ is [cyclic](c:cyclic-group) with generator $g$.

steps.slogan: Show that the generator of a simple abelian group has prime order.
steps.detail: Let $n=\operatorname{ord}(g)$. If $n=1$ then $G=1$ is not simple; if $n=\infty$ then $\langle g^2\rangle$ is proper and nontrivial; if $n=ab$ with $1<a<n$ then $\langle g^a\rangle$ has order $b$ and is proper and nontrivial. So $n=|G|$ is a [prime](c:prime-number).

steps.slogan: Show that every group of prime order is simple.
steps.detail: Let $|G|=p$ be prime and let $H\le G$. By Lagrange's theorem $|H|$ divides $p$, so $H=1$ or $H=G$, and every normal subgroup is one of these two. Also $G\ne 1$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: The step on prime order shows that a simple abelian group has prime order and is cyclic by the step before it. The converse step shows that prime order gives a simple group. Together, $G$ is simple exactly when $|G|$ is prime.

concepts.c:abelian-group: Commutativity turns every subgroup into a normal subgroup.
concepts.c:simple-group: Simplicity says that the only normal subgroups are $1$ and $G$.
concepts.c:prime-number: A prime has no divisors besides $1$ and itself, which excludes proper subgroups.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: A simple abelian group has one generator, so its subgroups are easy to list.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality of $\langle g\rangle$ lets simplicity force $\langle g\rangle=G$.
concepts.c:subgroup: Proper nontrivial subgroups of the cyclic group rule out composite order.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth projective [curve](c:algebraic-curve) over an algebraically closed field, with [canonical divisor](c:canonical-divisor) $K$. Let $D$ be an effective [divisor](c:divisor) that is special, that is $\ell(K-D)>0$. Then $\dim|D|\le\tfrac12\deg D$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a smooth projective [curve](c:algebraic-curve) of genus $g$ over an algebraically closed field.
The [divisor](c:divisor) $D$ is effective.
The divisor $D$ is special: $\ell(K-D)>0$.

conclusion: The complete linear system $|D|$ has dimension $\ell(D)-1\le\tfrac12\deg D$.

proofs.name: Linear systems add, then Riemann-Roch
proofs.slogan: Bound $\dim|D|+\dim|K-D|$ by $g-1$ with the sum map on linear systems, then subtract Riemann-Roch.
proofs.scope: The inequality only. The equality cases ($D=0$, $D=K$, and multiples of the hyperelliptic $g^1_2$) are not proved here.

roles.why: The curve gives finite dimensional spaces $H^0(\mathcal O(D))$, the canonical divisor with $\ell(K)=g$, and Riemann-Roch.
An effective divisor lies in its own [projective space](c:projective-space) $|D|$, which the sum map uses.
Speciality gives an effective divisor $E$ linearly equivalent to $K-D$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\dim|E+F|\ge\dim|E|+\dim|F|$ for effective divisors $E,F$.
steps.detail: Adding divisors gives a morphism $|E|\times|F|\to|E+F|$ of [projective spaces](c:projective-space). A divisor in $|E+F|$ splits into effective divisors of degrees $\deg E$ and $\deg F$ in finitely many ways, so the fibres are finite. A morphism of projective varieties with finite fibres preserves dimension, which gives the inequality.

steps.slogan: Pair $D$ with an effective divisor $E$ linearly equivalent to $K-D$.
steps.detail: Since $\ell(K-D)>0$, some effective $E$ satisfies $E\sim K-D$, so $D+E\sim K$ and $\dim|D+E|=\ell(K)-1=g-1$. The sum inequality gives $\dim|D|+\dim|E|\le g-1$, where $\dim|E|=\dim|K-D|$.

steps.slogan: Write the Riemann-Roch relation between $D$ and $K-D$.
steps.detail: Riemann-Roch says $\ell(D)-\ell(K-D)=\deg D+1-g$. Subtracting $1$ from both lengths gives $\dim|D|-\dim|K-D|=\deg D+1-g$.

steps.slogan: Add the inequality and the Riemann-Roch relation and divide by two.
steps.detail: Adding $\dim|D|+\dim|K-D|\le g-1$ and $\dim|D|-\dim|K-D|=\deg D+1-g$ cancels $\dim|K-D|$ and $g$. This leaves $2\dim|D|\le\deg D$.

concepts.c:algebraic-curve: Riemann-Roch and the canonical divisor are available on a smooth projective curve.
concepts.c:divisor: The divisor $D$ and its linear system $|D|$ carry the dimension count.
concepts.c:canonical-divisor: The canonical divisor $K$ has $\ell(K)=g$ and pairs $D$ with $K-D$.
concepts.c:projective-space: A complete linear system is a projective space, and the sum map joins such spaces.

source.note: Clifford's argument as in Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Chapter IV, Theorem 5.4.

statement: Let $R$ be a Noetherian [Cohen-Macaulay ring](c:cohen-macaulay-ring) and $I=(x_1,\dots,x_h)$ an ideal of [height](c:height) $h$. Then every [associated prime](c:associated-prime) of $R/I$ has height $h$. So $I$ has no embedded primes (Macaulay's unmixedness theorem).

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is Noetherian and [Cohen-Macaulay](c:cohen-macaulay-ring): every localization at a prime is a Cohen-Macaulay local ring.
The ideal $I$ is generated by $h$ elements and has [height](c:height) $h$.

conclusion: Every [associated prime](c:associated-prime) of $R/I$ has height exactly $h$.

proofs.name: Localize and use a regular sequence
proofs.slogan: Localize at an associated prime, show that the generators form a regular sequence, and compare depth with dimension.
proofs.scope: The ring $R$ need not be local, so the proof localizes at each associated prime. The converse, that unmixedness characterizes Cohen-Macaulay rings, is not proved.

roles.why: The localization $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$ is Cohen-Macaulay, so its parameters form a regular sequence and heights add to dimensions.
Generation by $h$ elements and height $h$ make the generators part of a system of parameters.

steps.slogan: Localize at an associated prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R/I$ to reach a local ring.
steps.detail: Let $\mathfrak p$ be an [associated prime](c:associated-prime) of $R/I$ and $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$ with $d=\dim A=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p$. Associated primes survive localization, so $\mathfrak pA$ is associated to $A/J$ with $J=IA$, and $\operatorname{depth}A/J=0$. The ideal $J$ has $h$ generators.

steps.slogan: Show that the localized ideal $J$ still has height $h$.
steps.detail: A prime of $A$ containing $J$ is $\mathfrak qA$ with $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak p$ a prime of $R$ containing $I$, so its [height](c:height) is at least $h$. Krull's height theorem gives $\operatorname{ht}J\le h$ because $J$ has $h$ generators. Hence $\operatorname{ht}J=h$.

steps.slogan: Extend the $h$ generators of $J$ to a system of parameters of $A$.
steps.detail: In a Cohen-Macaulay local ring $\operatorname{ht}J+\dim A/J=d$ for a proper ideal $J$, so $\dim A/J=d-h$. Choose $y_1,\dots,y_{d-h}$ whose images are parameters of $A/J$. Then $x_1,\dots,x_h,y_1,\dots,y_{d-h}$ generate an ideal primary to the maximal ideal, with $d$ generators.

steps.slogan: Show that $x_1,\dots,x_h$ is a [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence) in $A$.
steps.detail: In a Cohen-Macaulay local ring every system of parameters is a regular sequence (Matsumura, Theorem 17.4). An initial segment of a regular sequence is regular. Dividing by a regular sequence of length $h$ lowers [depth](c:depth) by $h$, so $\operatorname{depth}A/J=\operatorname{depth}A-h=d-h$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two values of the depth of $A/J$ to find $d=h$.
steps.detail: Step one gives $\operatorname{depth}A/J=0$ and the regular-sequence step gives $d-h$. So $d=h$, and $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}=d=h$.

concepts.c:cohen-macaulay-ring: Cohen-Macaulay localizations make parameters regular and give $\operatorname{ht}J+\dim A/J=\dim A$.
concepts.c:height: The height $h$ equals the number of generators, which makes them parameters.
concepts.c:associated-prime: An associated prime is where the quotient has depth $0$ after localizing.
concepts.c:regular-sequence: A regular sequence lowers depth by exactly its length.
concepts.c:depth: Depth $0$ at an associated prime forces the dimension to equal $h$.

source.note: Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, Theorem 17.6, with Theorem 17.4; also Bruns and Herzog, Cohen-Macaulay Rings, Theorem 2.1.6.

statement: A [metric space](c:metric-space) $X$ is [complete](c:complete-metric-space), meaning every [Cauchy filter](c:cauchy-filter) converges, if and only if every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) in $X$ converges.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a [metric space](c:metric-space) with metric $d$.

conclusion: Every Cauchy filter on $X$ converges if and only if every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the implication from convergent Cauchy sequences to completeness, for pseudometric spaces. The converse is the first step below.

proofs.name: Sequence from a Cauchy filter
proofs.slogan: Pick a point from each of nested small sets of the Cauchy filter, then show that its limit is the limit of the filter.
proofs.scope: Both directions. A [metric space](c:metric-space) has a countable base of balls, which makes the sequence argument possible; the empty space is trivially complete.

roles.why: The metric gives diameters of sets and balls, which define Cauchy filters and control the chosen sequence.

steps.slogan: Show that a Cauchy sequence generates a Cauchy filter.
steps.detail: Let $(x_k)$ be a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence). The sets $\{x_k:k\ge n\}$ generate a filter, and they have diameters tending to $0$, so it is a [Cauchy filter](c:cauchy-filter). If every Cauchy filter converges to $a$, then $x_k\to a$.

steps.slogan: Choose sets of small diameter inside a given Cauchy filter.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal F$ be a [Cauchy filter](c:cauchy-filter). For each $n\ge 1$ it contains a set $A_n$ with diameter below $1/n$. Replace $A_n$ by $A_1\cap\dots\cap A_n$ so the sets decrease; each is still in $\mathcal F$ and nonempty.

steps.slogan: Pick one point from each set and show that the picks form a Cauchy sequence.
steps.detail: Choose $x_n\in A_n$. For $m\ge n$ both $x_m$ and $x_n$ lie in $A_n$, so $d(x_m,x_n)<1/n$. Hence $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence.

steps.slogan: Show that the filter converges to the limit of the picked sequence.
steps.detail: By assumption $x_n\to a$. For $\varepsilon>0$ choose $n$ with $1/n<\varepsilon/2$ and $d(x_n,a)<\varepsilon/2$; then every $y\in A_n$ has $d(y,a)\le d(y,x_n)+d(x_n,a)<\varepsilon$. So the ball $B(a,\varepsilon)$ contains $A_n\in\mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F\to a$.

steps.slogan: Join the two implications into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: The tail step shows that completeness gives convergent Cauchy sequences. The limit step shows that convergent Cauchy sequences give convergent Cauchy filters. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:metric-space: Diameters and balls of the metric make small sets and convergence precise.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness is the property that the criterion reduces to sequences.
concepts.c:cauchy-filter: A Cauchy filter has sets of arbitrarily small diameter, which gives the sequence.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Cauchy sequences are the objects whose convergence the criterion requires.

source.note: mathlib chooses nested small sets (SequentiallyComplete.setSeq), picks a point in each, and uses cauchySeq_of_controlled and le_nhds_of_seq_tendsto_nhds.

statement: Let $OABC$ be a [tetrahedron](c:tetrahedron) whose three edges $OA,OB,OC$ at $O$ are pairwise [perpendicular](c:perpendicular). Then $[ABC]^2=[ABO]^2+[ACO]^2+[BCO]^2$, where $[\,\cdot\,]$ is the [area](c:area) of a face.

hypotheses.text: The points $O,A,B,C$ form a nondegenerate [tetrahedron](c:tetrahedron).
The edges $OA$, $OB$ and $OC$ are pairwise [perpendicular](c:perpendicular).

conclusion: The squared [area](c:area) of the face opposite $O$ equals the sum of the squared areas of the other three faces.

proofs.name: Coordinates and cross product
proofs.slogan: Put the right-angle corner at the origin, then compare the cross product of two edges with the three right-triangle areas.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for any lengths $a,b,c>0$ of the three perpendicular edges.

roles.why: Nondegeneracy gives positive edge lengths $a,b,c$.
Perpendicular edges let the three edges lie on the coordinate axes.

steps.slogan: Place $O$ at the origin and the points $A,B,C$ on the three axes.
steps.detail: Choose an orthonormal frame along $OA,OB,OC$. Then $A=(a,0,0)$, $B=(0,b,0)$ and $C=(0,0,c)$ with $a,b,c>0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the areas of the three faces that contain $O$.
steps.detail: Each such face is a right triangle whose legs are two of the edges at $O$. So $[ABO]=\tfrac12 ab$, $[ACO]=\tfrac12 ac$ and $[BCO]=\tfrac12 bc$.

steps.slogan: Compute the area of the face $ABC$ with the [cross product](c:cross-product).
steps.detail: The edge vectors are $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-a,b,0)$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=(-a,0,c)$. Their cross product is $(bc,ac,ab)$. So $[ABC]=\tfrac12\|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\|=\tfrac12\sqrt{b^2c^2+a^2c^2+a^2b^2}$.

steps.slogan: Square both sides and compare the three terms.
steps.detail: We have $[ABC]^2=\tfrac14\left(b^2c^2+a^2c^2+a^2b^2\right)=\left(\tfrac12 bc\right)^2+\left(\tfrac12 ac\right)^2+\left(\tfrac12 ab\right)^2$. By the face areas this is $[BCO]^2+[ACO]^2+[ABO]^2$.

concepts.c:tetrahedron: The corner $O$ and the opposite face $ABC$ are the parts of the tetrahedron compared.
concepts.c:perpendicular: Perpendicular edges allow the axis coordinates and right-triangle face areas.
concepts.c:area: The theorem compares squared areas of the four faces.
concepts.c:cross-product: The length of the cross product of two edges is twice the triangle's area.

source.note: Standard coordinate proof; the identity is the three-dimensional analogue of the Pythagorean theorem.

statement: Let $s$ be a finite set, let $f,g\colon s\to\mathbb R$ monovary ($g(i)<g(j)\Rightarrow f(i)\le f(j)$), and let $\sigma$ be a [permutation](c:permutation) of $s$. Then $\sum_i f(i)g(\sigma i)=\sum_i f(i)g(i)$ if and only if $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ monovary.

hypotheses.text: The index set $s$ is finite, so the sums are finite sums.
The functions $f$ and $g$ monovary on $s$: $g(i)<g(j)$ implies $f(i)\le f(j)$.
The map $\sigma$ is a [permutation](c:permutation) of $s$.

conclusion: The [sum](c:finite-sum) $\sum_i f(i)g(\sigma i)$ equals $\sum_i f(i)g(i)$ exactly when $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ monovary on $s$.

formal.difference: mathlib takes scalars from an ordered semiring acting on an ordered module, and a permutation of a larger index type that moves only points of $s$. This statement uses real numbers and a permutation of $s$.

proofs.name: Sandwich and swap
proofs.slogan: Sandwich the two sums by the rearrangement inequality, and show that a violating pair gains by a swap.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The empty set and one-point sets are trivial, since then every pair of functions monovary and both sums agree.

roles.why: Finite sums make the rearrangement inequality and the sum comparison meaningful.
Monovarying $f$ and $g$ give the inequality that bounds every permuted sum by the sorted sum.
The permutation $\sigma$ can be inverted, and a swap composed with it is again a permutation.

steps.slogan: Record the rearrangement inequality for $f,g$ and any permutation.
steps.detail: Since $f$ and $g$ monovary, $\sum_i f(i)g(\pi i)\le\sum_i f(i)g(i)$ for every permutation $\pi$ of $s$. This is the rearrangement inequality.

steps.slogan: Show that monovarying $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ forces equality of the two sums.
steps.detail: Apply the inequality to $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ with the permutation $\sigma^{-1}$. It gives $\sum_i f(i)g(i)\le\sum_i f(i)g(\sigma i)$. The first step gives the reverse inequality, so the sums are equal.

steps.slogan: Assume $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ do not monovary and pick a violating pair.
steps.detail: Then there are $x,y\in s$ with $g(\sigma x)<g(\sigma y)$ and $f(y)<f(x)$, and $x\ne y$. Let $\tau=\sigma\circ(x\;y)$, so $\tau x=\sigma y$, $\tau y=\sigma x$ and $\tau=\sigma$ elsewhere.

steps.slogan: Compute that $\tau$ gives a strictly larger sum than $\sigma$.
steps.detail: The two sums differ only at $x$ and $y$. Their difference is $f(x)g(\sigma y)+f(y)g(\sigma x)-f(x)g(\sigma x)-f(y)g(\sigma y)=(f(x)-f(y))(g(\sigma y)-g(\sigma x))>0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a violating pair makes the sum for $\sigma$ strictly smaller.
steps.detail: By the gain step and the rearrangement inequality for $\tau$, $\sum_i f(i)g(\sigma i)<\sum_i f(i)g(\tau i)\le\sum_i f(i)g(i)$. So equality of the two sums fails. This proves the forward direction by contraposition.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: The backward step shows that monovarying $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ gives equal sums. The forward step shows that equal sums give monovarying $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:permutation: The permuted sum, its inverse and the swap are all permutations of $s$.
concepts.c:finite-sum: The two sums being compared are finite sums over $s$.

source.note: mathlib uses MonovaryOn.sum_smul_comp_perm_le_sum_smul twice for the backward direction, and the permutation (Equiv.swap x y).trans σ for the forward direction.

statement: Let $r\ge 1$ and let $G$ be a finite graph of [maximum degree](c:maximum-degree) at most $r$ (Hajnal-Szemerédi). Then $G$ has a proper [colouring](c:graph-coloring) with $r+1$ colours whose colour classes differ in size by at most one. The same holds for every $k\ge r+1$ colours.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is finite.
Every vertex of $G$ has degree at most $r$, so $G$ has [maximum degree](c:maximum-degree) at most $r$.

conclusion: The graph $G$ has an equitable $(r+1)$-[colouring](c:graph-coloring): a proper colouring whose classes have sizes differing by at most $1$.

proofs.name: Nearly equitable colourings
proofs.slogan: Move vertices between colour classes along accessibility paths, and use induction on the part that cannot reach the small class.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Kierstead and Kostochka proof of the case of $r+1$ colours. A larger number $k$ of colours follows by replacing $r$ by $k-1$.

roles.why: Finiteness allows induction on the number of vertices and edges and the counting of class sizes.
A degree bound of $r$ gives a free class for a moved vertex and forces many neighbours across the split.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a graph whose number of vertices is divisible by $r+1$.
steps.detail: The cited proof first replaces $G$ by $G$ plus a disjoint clique with fewer than $r+1$ vertices, so that $|G|=s(r+1)$ and the maximum degree stays at most $r$. The clique vertices fall in distinct classes of an equitable colouring, so removing them keeps class sizes within one of each other.

steps.slogan: Delete an edge, colour the rest equitably, and move one endpoint to get a nearly equitable colouring.
steps.detail: By induction on the number of edges, $G-xy$ has an equitable $(r+1)$-[colouring](c:graph-coloring). If $x,y$ lie in different classes, the colouring is proper for $G$. Otherwise some class $W$ has no neighbour of $x$, and moving $x$ to $W$ gives a colouring with one class of size $s-1$ ($V^-$), one of size $s+1$ ($V^+$) and the rest of size $s$.

steps.slogan: Join classes by arcs when a vertex can move across, and shift vertices along a path.
steps.detail: Put an arc $V\to W$ when some vertex of $V$ has no neighbour in $W$. If $V^-$ is reachable from $V^+$, move one vertex along each arc of a shortest path from $V^+$ to $V^-$. Every class then has size $s$, which gives an equitable colouring.

steps.slogan: Otherwise split the classes into those that reach $V^-$ and those that do not.
steps.detail: Let $A$ be the set of $a$ classes that reach $V^-$ and $B$ the other $b=r+1-a$ classes, with $V^+\in B$. No arc leaves $B$ for $A$, so each vertex of $B$ has a neighbour in every class of $A$. Hence it has at least $a$ neighbours in $A$ and at most $b-1$ inside $B$.

steps.slogan: Move one vertex from $B$ to $A$, then colour the two parts equitably.
steps.detail: The cited proof counts edges between the two parts to find a vertex $y$ of $B$ that can enter a class of $A$ after a shift along a path in $A$, so that $A$ again has all classes of size $s$. The part $B-y$ has $bs$ vertices and maximum degree below $b$, so induction gives an equitable $b$-colouring with classes of size $s$. Together the two colourings are equitable.

concepts.c:maximum-degree: A bound on the degree gives a free class and controls neighbours across the split.
concepts.c:graph-coloring: Moving a vertex to a class without its neighbours keeps the colouring proper.

source.ref: H. A. Kierstead and A. V. Kostochka, A short proof of the Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem on equitable colouring, Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 17 (2008), 265-270.
source.note: Shorter proof of the theorem of A. Hajnal and E. Szemerédi (Combinatorial theory and its applications II, 1970, 601-623); the steps outline the nearly equitable colouring argument.

statement: Let $G$ be a topological group and $e\colon Y\to Z$ a $G$-map of [$G$-CW complexes](c:g-cw-complex). If $e^H\colon Y^H\to Z^H$ is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence) on [fixed points](c:fixed-point-space-2) for every closed subgroup $H\le G$, then $e$ is a $G$-[homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence).

hypotheses.text: $Y$ and $Z$ are [G-CW complexes](c:g-cw-complex) and $e\colon Y\to Z$ is a $G$-map.
For every closed subgroup $H\le G$ the map $e^H\colon Y^H\to Z^H$ on [fixed points](c:fixed-point-space-2) is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence).

conclusion: There is a $G$-map $h\colon Z\to Y$ with $eh\simeq_G\mathrm{id}_Z$ and $he\simeq_G\mathrm{id}_Y$.

proofs.name: Cell-by-cell lifting
proofs.slogan: Lift maps cell by cell through fixed-point spaces, then run the classical Whitehead argument with $X=Z$ and $X=Y$.
proofs.scope: Equivariant homotopies are $G$-maps $X\times I\to Y$ with trivial action on $I$. The converse, that a $G$-homotopy equivalence is one on every $H$-fixed point space, is immediate and not proved here.

roles.why: The cells $G/H\times D^n$ allow induction over cells, and the same lifting applies to $X=Z$, $X=Y$ and $X\times I$.
A weak equivalence on each fixed-point space $Y^H\to Z^H$ solves the lifting problem for each cell of orbit type $G/H$.

steps.slogan: Turn the lifting problem on a cell $G/H\times D^n$ into one for $e^H$.
steps.detail: A $G$-map $G/H\times D^n\to Y$ is determined by its restriction to $eH\times D^n$, which is a map $D^n\to Y^H$. Conversely every map $D^n\to Y^H$ extends uniquely to a $G$-map. So a lifting problem for $G/H\times(D^n,S^{n-1})$ against $e$ is a lifting problem for $(D^n,S^{n-1})$ against $e^H$.

steps.slogan: Solve each cell problem and assemble a lift over a relative G-CW complex.
steps.detail: Since $e^H$ is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence), each cell problem has a solution up to homotopy rel boundary, by the classical lifting property. Induction over the cells of a relative $G$-CW complex $(X,A)$ with the homotopy extension property gives: if $h\colon A\to Y$ and $g\colon X\to Z$ satisfy $eh=g|_A$, then $h$ extends to $h'\colon X\to Y$ with $eh'\simeq_G g$ rel $A$.

steps.slogan: Show that composing with $e$ is a bijection $[X,Y]_G\to[X,Z]_G$ for every G-CW complex $X$.
steps.detail: Surjectivity is the lift step with $A=\varnothing$. For injectivity, given $h_0,h_1\colon X\to Y$ and a $G$-homotopy $eh_0\simeq eh_1$, apply the lift step to $(X\times I,X\times\partial I)$ with $h_0,h_1$ on the ends. The lift is a $G$-homotopy $h_0\simeq h_1$.

steps.slogan: Take $X=Z$ to get a right inverse of $e$ up to homotopy.
steps.detail: Since $[Z,Y]_G\to[Z,Z]_G$ is onto, the class of $\mathrm{id}_Z$ comes from some $G$-map $h\colon Z\to Y$. So $eh\simeq_G\mathrm{id}_Z$.

steps.slogan: Take $X=Y$ and compare $e(he)$ with $e$ to get a left inverse.
steps.detail: In $[Y,Z]_G$ we have $e(he)=(eh)e\simeq e=e\,\mathrm{id}_Y$. Since $[Y,Y]_G\to[Y,Z]_G$ is injective, $he\simeq_G\mathrm{id}_Y$. With the previous step, $e$ is a $G$-[homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence).

concepts.c:g-cw-complex: Its cells $G/H\times D^n$ reduce each lifting problem to a fixed-point space.
concepts.c:weak-homotopy-equivalence: Weak equivalence of $e^H$ is what solves the nonequivariant lifting problem for each cell.
concepts.c:fixed-point-space-2: Equivariant maps out of $G/H\times D^n$ land in the fixed-point space $Y^H$.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The conclusion is an equivariant homotopy inverse, built from the two bijections.

source.note: The classical route of Matumoto (1971), Illman (1972) and Waner (1980): an equivariant lifting lemma, then the Whitehead argument with X = Z and X = Y.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with [circumcircle](c:circumcircle) of radius $R$ and center $O$, and [incircle](c:incircle) of radius $r$ and center $I$. Then $OI^2=R(R-2r)$, equivalently $\frac1{R-OI}+\frac1{R+OI}=\frac1r$. In particular $R\ge 2r$.

hypotheses.text: The points $A,B,C$ form a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle) with angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

proofs.name: Power of the incenter
proofs.slogan: Cut the circumcircle by the bisector from $A$ and compute the power of the incenter in two ways.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every triangle. The two equivalent forms and $R\ge 2r$ follow in the last step.

roles.why: The triangle supplies its bisector from $A$, the incircle tangent points and the circumcircle through $A,B,C$.

steps.slogan: Extend the [angle bisector](c:angle-bisector) from $A$ through $I$ to meet the circumcircle at $L$.
steps.detail: The incenter $I$ lies on the bisector of angle $A$ and inside the circumcircle. The bisector meets the circle again at $L$, on the arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Then $\angle BAL=\angle LAC=\alpha/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $LB=LI$ by comparing two angles of triangle $LBI$.
steps.detail: The [inscribed angle](c:inscribed-angle) $\angle LBC$ equals $\angle LAC=\alpha/2$ and $\angle CBI=\beta/2$, so $\angle LBI=(\alpha+\beta)/2$. The exterior angle of triangle $ABI$ at $I$ gives $\angle BIL=\alpha/2+\beta/2$. Equal angles at $B$ and $I$ give $LB=LI$.

steps.slogan: Compute the [chord](c:chord) $LB$ as $2R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}$.
steps.detail: The chord $LB$ of the circumcircle subtends the inscribed angle $\angle BAL=\alpha/2$ at $A$. By the extended law of sines in triangle $ABL$, $LB=2R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}$.

steps.slogan: Compute $IA$ as $r/\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}$ in the right triangle with the tangent point.
steps.detail: Let $F$ be the point where the incircle touches $AB$. Then $IF=r$, $IF\perp AB$ and $\angle IAF=\alpha/2$. So $IA=r/\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}$.

steps.slogan: Apply the intersecting chords theorem to the chord $AL$ through $I$.
steps.detail: The line $OI$ meets the circumcircle in two points at distances $R-d$ and $R+d$ from $I$. The chord $AL$ passes through $I$ as well. So $IA\cdot IL=(R-d)(R+d)=R^2-d^2$.

steps.slogan: Equate the two values of $IA\cdot IL$ and solve for $d^2$.
steps.detail: Since $IL=LB$, we get $IA\cdot IL=\frac{r}{\sin(\alpha/2)}\cdot 2R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}=2Rr$. With the power step, $R^2-d^2=2Rr$, so $d^2=R(R-2r)$. Also $\frac1{R-d}+\frac1{R+d}=\frac{2R}{R^2-d^2}=\frac1r$, and $d^2\ge 0$ gives $R\ge 2r$.

concepts.c:circumcircle: Its radius $R$ and center $O$ give the power of the point $I$.
concepts.c:incircle: Its radius $r$ gives $IA$ through a right triangle at the tangent point.
concepts.c:triangle: The angles of the triangle fix the bisector and the half-angle values.
concepts.c:angle-bisector: The bisector from $A$ carries $I$ and meets the circumcircle at $L$.
concepts.c:inscribed-angle: Inscribed angles on the same arc give the angles at $B$ in triangle $LBI$.
concepts.c:chord: The chord $LB$ has length $2R\sin(\alpha/2)$ by its inscribed angle.

source.note: Standard proof by the power of the incenter, as in the classical treatments of Euler's formula.

statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup) of a group $G$, [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-group) of class at most $m$ and $n$. Then $MN$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, nilpotent of class at most $m+n$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ and $N$ are [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$.
$M$ is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-group) of class at most $m$ and $N$ of class at most $n$, so $\gamma_{m+1}(M)=1=\gamma_{n+1}(N)$.

conclusion: $MN$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ and $\gamma_{m+n+1}(MN)=1$.

proofs.name: Count commutator weights
proofs.slogan: Show that every long commutator in $M\cup N$ lies deep in the lower central series of $M$ or of $N$.
proofs.scope: All $m,n\ge 0$, where class $0$ means the trivial group. Here $\gamma_1(H)=H$, $\gamma_{i+1}(H)=[\gamma_i(H),H]$ and $[a,b]=a^{-1}b^{-1}ab$.

roles.why: Normality makes $MN$ a normal subgroup, puts each $\gamma_i(M)$ normal in $G$, and gives $[N,M]\le M\cap N$.
The class bounds say that $\gamma_{m+1}(M)$ and $\gamma_{n+1}(N)$ are trivial, so deep enough commutators vanish.

steps.slogan: Show that $MN$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
steps.detail: Since $M$ is normal, $MN=NM$, so $MN$ is a subgroup. For $g\in G$ we have $g(MN)g^{-1}=(gMg^{-1})(gNg^{-1})=MN$. So $MN$ is normal.

steps.slogan: Reduce $\gamma_{m+n+1}(MN)=1$ to long left-normed [commutators](c:group-commutator) of elements of $M\cup N$.
steps.detail: The group $MN$ is generated by $M\cup N$, which is closed under inverses. In a group generated by a set $X$, the term $\gamma_k$ of the [lower central series](c:lower-central-series) is the normal closure of the commutators $[y_1,\dots,y_k]$ with $y_i\in X$. So it suffices to show $[y_1,\dots,y_{m+n+1}]=1$ for all $y_i\in M\cup N$.

steps.slogan: Label each entry $y_i$ by $M$ or $N$ and count the labels.
steps.detail: Label every $y_i$ by a subgroup that contains it. Let $p$ entries carry the label $M$ and $q$ the label $N$, with $p+q=m+n+1$. Then $p\ge m+1$ or $q\ge n+1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the commutator lies in $\gamma_p(M)$, and by symmetry in $\gamma_q(N)$.
steps.detail: Put $c_t=[y_1,\dots,y_t]$. Before the first $M$-label $c_t\in N$, so the first $M$-entry gives $c_t\in[N,M]\le M=\gamma_1(M)$ (or $c_1=y_1\in M$). After that, an $N$-entry keeps $c_t$ in the same normal subgroup $\gamma_i(M)$ and an $M$-entry moves it into $\gamma_{i+1}(M)$, so $c_k\in\gamma_p(M)$, and likewise $c_k\in\gamma_q(N)$.

steps.slogan: Use the class bounds to make the commutator trivial and finish.
steps.detail: If $p\ge m+1$ then $\gamma_p(M)\le\gamma_{m+1}(M)=1$, and if $q\ge n+1$ then $\gamma_q(N)=1$. So $[y_1,\dots,y_{m+n+1}]=1$ and $\gamma_{m+n+1}(MN)=1$. With normality of $MN$ this is the theorem.

concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality of $M$ and $N$ gives $[N,M]\le M\cap N$ and normal terms $\gamma_i(M)$.
concepts.c:nilpotent-group: Class bounds make deep terms of the lower central series trivial.
concepts.c:group-commutator: Long left-normed commutators of generators generate the deep terms of the series.
concepts.c:lower-central-series: The class is read from the first trivial term of the lower central series.

source.note: Textbook argument with left-normed commutators; compare Robinson, A Course in the Theory of Groups, Section 5.2.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group with $k$ [conjugacy classes](c:conjugacy-class). Over $\mathbb C$, its [group determinant](c:group-determinant) $\Theta_G=\det(x_{gh^{-1}})_{g,h\in G}$ equals $\prod_{i=1}^k\Theta_i^{d_i}$. The $\Theta_i=\det\sum_g x_g\rho_i(g)$ are pairwise non-proportional [irreducible polynomials](c:irreducible-polynomial), and $d_i$ is the degree of the [irreducible representation](c:irreducible-representation) $\rho_i$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is finite, so $\mathbb C[G]$ is finite dimensional and the $|G|$ variables $x_g$ are finitely many.

conclusion: The [group determinant](c:group-determinant) factors into $k$ pairwise non-proportional irreducible polynomials, one for each irreducible representation, each with exponent equal to its degree.

proofs.name: Wedderburn decomposition
proofs.slogan: Write the group determinant as a determinant on the group algebra, split the algebra into matrix algebras, and read off the factors.
proofs.scope: Complex coefficients and the variables $x_g$ as indeterminates. The count $k$ of irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes, as the center of the algebra shows.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) finite dimensional and semisimple, so it splits into matrix algebras.

steps.slogan: Write $\Theta_G$ as the determinant of left multiplication by the generic element.
steps.detail: Let $X=\sum_g x_g\,g$ in $\mathbb C[x_g][G]$. In the basis $G$, left multiplication by $X$ has matrix entries $x_{gh^{-1}}$. So $\Theta_G=\det L_X$.

steps.slogan: Split the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) into matrix algebras and factor the determinant.
steps.detail: By Maschke's theorem and the Artin-Wedderburn theorem, $\mathbb C[G]\cong\prod_{i} M_{d_i}(\mathbb C)$ with one factor per irreducible representation. The center has the $k$ class sums as a basis and has dimension equal to the number of factors, so there are $k$ factors. The left regular representation is $\bigoplus_i\rho_i^{\,d_i}$, so $\det L_X=\prod_i\Theta_i^{d_i}$.

steps.slogan: Show that each $\Theta_i$ is an [irreducible polynomial](c:irreducible-polynomial).
steps.detail: The linear map $(x_g)\mapsto\sum_g x_g\rho_i(g)$ is onto $M_{d_i}(\mathbb C)$, so after a linear change of variables $\Theta_i$ is a generic $d_i\times d_i$ determinant. That determinant is irreducible: in a factorization $fg$ each variable lies in one factor, and two entries of one row in different factors would give a monomial with two entries from one row, which $\det$ lacks.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Theta_i$ and $\Theta_j$ are not proportional for $i\ne j$.
steps.detail: Take $X\in\mathbb C[G]$ whose $i$-th matrix component is singular and whose other components are identity matrices. Then $\Theta_i(X)=0$ and $\Theta_j(X)=1$. So the two polynomials have different zero sets.

steps.slogan: Read the factorization in the polynomial ring as the irreducible factorization.
steps.detail: The ring $\mathbb C[x_g]$ is a unique factorization domain. The product $\prod_i\Theta_i^{d_i}$ has $k$ irreducible, pairwise non-proportional factors, so it is the irreducible factorization of $\Theta_G$ with exponents $d_i$.

concepts.c:conjugacy-class: The number of conjugacy classes equals the number of irreducible factors.
concepts.c:group-determinant: The group determinant is the polynomial that the proof factors.
concepts.c:irreducible-polynomial: Each factor $\Theta_i$ is shown irreducible, which fixes the factorization.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Each irreducible representation gives one factor, with exponent its degree.
concepts.c:group-algebra: Its matrix-algebra decomposition turns the determinant into a product.

source.note: Standard proof through the Wedderburn decomposition of the complex group algebra.

statement: Let $K$ be a field and $A=K\langle x_1,\dots,x_d\rangle/(f_1,\dots,f_r)$ a [graded algebra](c:graded-algebra), where $f_j$ is homogeneous of degree at least $2$ and $r_i$ of them have degree $i$. Put $P(t)=1-dt+\sum_i r_it^i$. Then $H_A(t)P(t)-1$ has nonnegative coefficients, where $H_A$ is the Hilbert series. So $A$ is infinite dimensional if $P(t_0)\le 0$ for some $t_0>0$.

hypotheses.text: $A$ is the quotient of the [free algebra](c:free-algebra) $T=K\langle x_1,\dots,x_d\rangle$ by the ideal generated by homogeneous $f_1,\dots,f_r$ of degree at least $2$.
For the last claim only: $P(t_0)\le 0$ for some real $t_0>0$.

conclusion: The Hilbert series satisfies $H_A(t)P(t)\ge 1$ coefficientwise, and $A$ is infinite dimensional whenever $P(t_0)\le 0$ for some $t_0>0$.

proofs.name: Relation module and Hilbert series
proofs.slogan: Compare the Hilbert series of the augmentation ideal, a quotient of a free module, with the module of relations generated by the $f_j$.
proofs.scope: The algebraic inequality and its consequence for dimension; for example $r\le d^2/4$ quadratic relations give $P(2/d)\le 0$. The uses for $p$-groups and class field towers apply this to group algebras and are not proved here.

roles.why: The presentation gives a free module $A\otimes V$ mapping onto $A_+$ and a kernel generated by the images of the $f_j$.
A value $P(t_0)\le0$ contradicts the inequality $H_A(t_0)P(t_0)\ge1$ for a finite dimensional $A$.

steps.slogan: Present the augmentation ideal $A_+$ as a quotient of the free module $A\otimes V$.
steps.detail: Let $V=\operatorname{span}(x_i)$ in degree $1$. The map $\mu\colon A\otimes V\to A_+$, $a\otimes x\mapsto ax$, is a surjection of graded left $A$-modules. For $N=\ker\mu$ the Hilbert series satisfy $H_N=dt\,H_A-(H_A-1)$.

steps.slogan: Define the relation map $\varphi$ on the ideal $I$ and show that $\varphi(I)=N$.
steps.detail: Every $f\in T_+$ is uniquely $\sum g_ix_i$; put $\varphi(f)=\sum\bar g_i\otimes x_i$, a left $T$-linear map with $\mu\varphi(f)=\bar f$, so $\varphi(I)\subseteq N$. Conversely an element $\sum a_i\otimes x_i$ of $N$ with lifts $g_i$ has $\sum g_ix_i\in I$, so $N=\varphi(I)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $N$ is generated by the $r$ elements $\varphi(f_j)$.
steps.detail: Write $I=\sum_jTf_j+\sum_jTf_jT_+$. For $v=v'x_k$ we get $\varphi(uf_jv)=\overline{uf_jv'}\otimes x_k=0$ since $f_j\in I$, so $N=\sum_jA\,\varphi(f_j)$ with $\varphi(f_j)$ of degree $\deg f_j$. Hence $H_N\le H_A\sum_ir_it^i$ coefficientwise.

steps.slogan: Combine the two Hilbert series bounds into $H_AP\ge 1$.
steps.detail: The first step gives $H_N=dtH_A-H_A+1$ and the third gives $H_N\le H_A\sum_ir_it^i$. So $1\le H_A(1-dt+\sum_ir_it^i)=H_AP$ coefficientwise.

steps.slogan: Evaluate at $t_0$ to show that a finite dimensional $A$ is impossible.
steps.detail: If $A$ is finite dimensional, $H_A$ is a polynomial with constant term $1$ and nonnegative coefficients, so $H_A(t_0)>0$. The polynomial $H_AP-1$ has nonnegative coefficients, so $H_A(t_0)P(t_0)\ge1$. But $P(t_0)\le0$ gives $H_A(t_0)P(t_0)\le 0$, a contradiction.

concepts.c:graded-algebra: Grading by degree gives the Hilbert series that the inequality compares.
concepts.c:free-algebra: The free algebra supplies the unique decomposition $f=\sum g_ix_i$ used by $\varphi$.

source.note: Direct version of the Golod-Shafarevich inequality (Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat. 28, 1964), in the short algebraic form of Vinberg (Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat. 29, 1965).

statement: Let $X$ be a compact [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) of genus $g\ge 2$. Its group of orientation-preserving conformal automorphisms is finite, of order at most $84(g-1)$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a compact [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface).
The [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) of $X$ is $g\ge 2$.

proofs.name: Quotient and Riemann-Hurwitz
proofs.slogan: Quotient by the finite automorphism group, apply the Riemann-Hurwitz formula, and bound the orbifold Euler characteristic from below by $1/42$.
proofs.scope: Whole theorem, including finiteness. The equality case, the Hurwitz groups, is not treated here.

roles.why: Compactness gives the quotient surface and the Riemann-Hurwitz count for a finite branched cover.
Genus at least $2$ makes the Lefschetz count negative, so the action is faithful, and makes $2g-2>0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\operatorname{Aut}(X)$ is finite by its action on $H^1(X,\mathbb Z)$.
steps.detail: Automorphisms preserve the positive definite form $\int\alpha\wedge{*\beta}$ on $H^1(X,\mathbb R)$ and the lattice $H^1(X,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^{2g}$. Only finitely many integer matrices preserve such a form. The action is faithful: a nonidentity automorphism has a nonnegative number of fixed points, but acting trivially on $H^1$ would give the Lefschetz number $2-2g<0$.

steps.slogan: Form the quotient map $\pi\colon X\to Y=X/G$ and record its ramification.
steps.detail: The quotient $Y$ is a compact Riemann surface of some genus $h$, and $\pi$ has degree $|G|$. It branches over finitely many points $y_1,\dots,y_k$. Over $y_i$ lie $|G|/m_i$ points, each with ramification index $m_i$ equal to the order of its cyclic stabilizer.

steps.slogan: Apply the Riemann-Hurwitz formula to the map $\pi$.
steps.detail: The formula reads $2g-2=|G|(2h-2)+\sum_x(e_x-1)$. The points over $y_i$ contribute $\frac{|G|}{m_i}(m_i-1)$. So $2g-2=|G|\,\mu$ with $\mu=2h-2+\sum_{i=1}^k\big(1-\frac1{m_i}\big)$.

steps.slogan: Show by cases that the positive number $\mu$ is at least $1/42$.
steps.detail: Here $\mu>0$ since $g\ge2$. If $h\ge2$ then $\mu\ge2$, and if $h=1$ then $k\ge1$ and $\mu\ge\frac12$. If $h=0$ then $k\ge3$, with $\mu\ge\frac12$ for $k\ge5$ and $\mu\ge\frac16$ for $k=4$; for $k=3$, $\mu=1-\sum\frac1{m_i}$ has least positive value $1-\frac12-\frac13-\frac17=\frac1{42}$.

steps.slogan: Divide $2g-2$ by $\mu$ to bound the order of the group.
steps.detail: We have $|G|=\frac{2g-2}{\mu}\le 42(2g-2)=84(g-1)$. Finiteness of $G$ comes from the first step.

concepts.c:riemann-surface: Quotients and branched covers of compact Riemann surfaces are again compact Riemann surfaces.
concepts.c:genus-of-a-surface: The genus enters the Riemann-Hurwitz count and makes $2g-2$ positive.

source.note: The classical proof of Hurwitz (Math. Ann. 41, 1893, 403-442): quotient by the automorphism group and Riemann-Hurwitz.
